raw_comment:
I notice that men make almost all of the money. This isn't surprising, but it's still sad and unfair. I also notice that men's basketball and football make over half of the money, even though they are only two sports out of 29 listed. 
    I wonder why men's volleyball players make about a tenth of what women's volleyball players make. People likely watch more women's volleyball, and I wonder why this is. Men's gymnastics also makes a lot less than women's gymnastics.
    This relates to me and my community because in almost all situations, women make less than men playing the same sports. The issue of making less money for the same thing affects me and many other girls and women worldwide. 
    Title: "The Pay Gap is Still Here, and it's not Small"

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
1. This graph depicts the average earnings of college athletes involved in a various range of sports. I noticed that the left side of the graph, with only four sports, conveys far greater earnings than any sports listed on the right-hand graph. I was surprised that women's sports were pretty concentrated near the top on the right-hand graph. I was really happy to see this, as I have always felt like female sports don't usually get the love that they deserve. On a similar note, I found it interesting that women's basketball was on the left-hand of the graph (earning a much higher amount). While it is still significantly lower than men's basketball, it is a very high earning for a college athlete, and I was unaware that their earnings were so much higher than that of a majority of men's college sports like track or ice hockey.
    2. I wonder why men's soccer is so low. Every time the World Cup comes around, the world becomes infatuated with male soccer players such as Messi or Ronaldo. For that reason, I find it surprising that men's soccer at the college level is relatively unpopular. 
    3. This relates to me as a senior in high school because while I am not personally an athlete, I have a lot of classmates and peers announcing their commitments to further their athletic careers in their college endeavors. I found this a very interesting statistic to look at, given I might know a person or two who will contribute to these numbers one day.
    4. College Athletes: Is the Work Worth it?

raw_comment:
Sportularity; The earning of college athletes, does popularity contribute?
    The graph is showing the earnings of college athletes in certain sports. One big thing that I notice is that sports that are also played on a professional level, like football and basketball, they tend to make so much more than the other sports below them. I assume that this is because most college athletes do want to go on and play at these higher levels. I can also make the assumption that these sports make more because they're more popular in the entertainment industry. This is also very well seen where it says "Men and women's track saw in increase after getting exposure in the Olympics," which is pretty much the ultimate sports competition and centers of entertainment.
    I wonder if this graph would differ in other countries like Europe, where soccer is a more popular sport, where would soccer stand on this graph (If this graph's statistics are taken from American colleges of course.)
    This can connect to the community because sports is one of the biggest entertainment industries in America. I know even my family partake in watching football or going out to watch other sports. We know which sports are more popular because us ourselves watch them constantly.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Two-panel horizontal bar chart** (ranked bar charts).
- Left panel: major sports.
- Right panel: “nonrevenue” sports.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Side-by-side panels / small multiples** by sport group (“major sports” vs. “nonrevenue” sports).
- Within each panel, bars are **not stacked**.
- Bars are **sorted/ranked** by earnings.
- A few bars in the right panel are **highlighted with color** and accompanied by an **annotation arrow/text**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels next to bars |
| Average earnings | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis |
| Sport group (major sports vs. “nonrevenue” sports) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel titles |
| Highlighted sports status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (red vs. light gray/white) |

Notes:
- The highlighted bars correspond to specific sports visible in the right panel, but the visualization encodes this primarily through **color**, not a separate legend.
- The annotation text and arrow are explanatory callouts, not additional plotted data variables.
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that both women's and men's basketball are classified as major sports, though male basketball players make significantly more than women. Men's basketball athletes make the most, with over 600,000 annually. Major sports seem to be the ones with the most media publicity. Many sports have higher earnings for one gender vs. the other, such as women's vs men's gymnastics, in which women athletes make more. I noticed that track/cross country athletes have earned more since gaining exposure from the Olympics. Its important to note these are the expected earnings, not the current ones. 
    2. I wonder how this data compares to women's earnings in previous years. What role does social media play in athlete's salaries? Is it wrong to pay people based on popularity rather than skill?
    3. This doesn't closely collect to me because I do not watch sports or have family members who are college athletes. 
    4. The Race of Revenues: Projected College Athlete Earnings

raw_comment:
Headline: Sports They Play, But What About the Pay?
    
    What do you notice?
    I noticed that there is a massive pay gap between athletes in major sports and those in non-revenue sports. The highest-paying major sport is men's basketball, at over $600,000, while the highest-paying nonrevenue sport is men's golf, at just over $20,000. I also noticed that while women's and men's basketball are both major sports, women get paid over $500,000 less than men. This shows that the gender pay gap is also relevant to college sports. The final thing I noticed is that women's and men's track/cross-country pay increased because of the Olympics. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why some sports have higher pay for men than others for women. Why is the gap between major and nonrevenue sports so extreme? Are these earnings based on media attention? Why didn't any other sports, such as women's gymnastics, increase pay after the Olympics life track/cross country? 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me and my community because my friends and I all play sports, and I know some of them want to play in college. It's interesting to see the average pay between different sports like women's tennis and women's soccer, for example.

raw_comment:
Observations - This graph shows the average earnings of college athletes in major and non-revenue sports. Among the major sports sections, the average earning of college athletes in Men’s basketball is the highest, well over $600,000, while Baseball is the lowest, with numbers under $100,000. In non revenue sports, men’s golf and women’s gymnastics are among the highest, though men’s track/cross country and women’s track/cross country had a sharp rise in earnings.

    Headline - Track to Triumph: College Athletes' Earnings To Take Off?

## 1. Chart type
- **Two-panel horizontal bar chart** (ranked bar charts).
- Left panel: major sports.
- Right panel: “nonrevenue” sports.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Side-by-side panels / small multiples** by sport group (“major sports” vs. “nonrevenue” sports).
- Within each panel, bars are **not stacked**.
- Bars are **sorted/ranked** by earnings.
- A few bars in the right panel are **highlighted with color** and accompanied by an **annotation arrow/text**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels next to bars |
| Average earnings | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis |
| Sport group (major sports vs. “nonrevenue” sports) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel titles |
| Highlighted sports status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (red vs. light gray/white) |

Notes:
- The highlighted bars correspond to specific sports visible in the right panel, but the visualization encodes this primarily through **color**, not a separate legend.
- The annotation text and arrow are explanatory callouts, not additional plotted data variables.
raw_comment: This graph shows the average earnings of both college athletes in major sports and "nonrevenue" sports. I noticed that men's basketball makes a significant amount more money than women's basketball. I also noticed fencing and rifle make little to no money at all. I've never heard of rifle and fencing isn't very popular so this makes sense. I wonder why men's golf makes so much more money compared to other non-revenue sports. I also wonder if Division 1 teams make significantly more money compared to Division 2 and 3 teams. This relates to me and my community because I love watching sports and playing sports. Some people I know want to play a sport in college so this can also impact them.

raw_comment:
This graph analyzes the earnings of college athletes in both major revenue sports and non-revenue sports. The major revenue sports, which include men's basketball, football, baseball, and women's basketball, show a significant pay gap between men and women, with men’s basketball earning much more than women’s basketball. In contrast, on the non-revenue side, men’s golf stands out as the highest-earning non-revenue sport, even though it doesn’t generate nearly as much revenue as the major sports. Women's gymnastics earns much more than men’s gymnastics, and men’s and women’s track and cross-country sports are on the rise in earnings, largely due to increased exposure from the Olympics. Fencing, on the other hand, generates the least revenue of all the sports listed. I wonder why softball, which is often considered the counterpart to baseball, is classified as a non-revenue sport while baseball is a major sport. I also wonder how the earnings of these sports have changed over time and if the financial gap between men’s and women’s sports will continue to persist as women’s sports gain more exposure. Additionally, I wonder how increased media coverage and sponsorship deals have influenced the revenue disparity. This graph is relevant to my community because college sports are widely followed, and this analysis offers a new perspective on how these athletes are compensated.
    Headline: The Financial Divide in College Sports

raw_comment: I noticed that basketball and football tend to make the most money. Men's basketball is making more than football by approximately $200,000. I thought that this difference was interesting because I considered football to be the bigger sport, and I feel as though I have heard more articles about NIL in football. I then started to wonder if this difference was because a basketball roster typically includes around 15 athletes, while a football roster contains around 52. I wondered if this difference in average would change when only the average earnings of athletes who started for their respective teams are recorded. This relates to my community because I go to a college where some of my classmates are athletes who have NIL opportunities. A good name might be, "How much do athletes in popular sports make compared to their less popular colleagues through NIL?"

raw_comment:
In this graph comparing the earnings of nonrevenue and revenue college sports, I noticed a couple of huge differences. First, men's basketball earns an average of $600,000, which is 200x larger than the average earnings of fencing, which is around $3,000. Then, I also noticed the NAIA was only passed 5 years ago, meaning all of this money has shot up to rapid numbers in such a short period. Finally, I saw that women's basketball brings in almost $200,000 less than men's basketball; however, many women's sports on the nonrevenue side "beat" men's sports in earnings. I am curious what caused these earnings to skyrocket so quickly in the last five years, and what brings in the most money to these groups. I also wonder if any other sports will experience growth like track and field did because of the coverage from the Olympics (if so, what sport?). This relates to me because as a student-athlete I am surrounded by the environment of people committing to specific colleges, which comes with potential financial earnings. 
    Headline: The Rising Earnings of College Athletes

1. Men’s basketball is the highest-paying sport in college while fencing is the lowest. Some sports have large gender pay gaps while others are relatively similar. Only two of the nonrevenue sports, men’s golf, and women’s gymnastics, make over 20k on average.

    4. The Price of Being the Best- How Much Do College Athletes Make in Their Sports?

    I notice that the sports which receives the least fundings are fencing, rifle, and men's volleyball. This relates to me and my community because a lot of people I know have been recruited to play sports at certain colleges therefore this graph affects them.

- **Two-panel horizontal bar chart** (ranked bar charts).
- Left panel: major sports.
- Right panel: “nonrevenue” sports.

- **Side-by-side panels / small multiples** by sport group (“major sports” vs. “nonrevenue” sports).
- Within each panel, bars are **not stacked**.
- Bars are **sorted/ranked** by earnings.
- A few bars in the right panel are **highlighted with color** and accompanied by an **annotation arrow/text**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels next to bars |
| Average earnings | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis |
| Sport group (major sports vs. “nonrevenue” sports) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel titles |
| Highlighted sports status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (red vs. light gray/white) |

- The highlighted bars correspond to specific sports visible in the right panel, but the visualization encodes this primarily through **color**, not a separate legend.
- The annotation text and arrow are explanatory callouts, not additional plotted data variables.

Which is a great difference compared to the earning of athletes in major sports, with Men’s Basketball reaching $600,000.  I also notice that the major sports category has substantially less sports than the “nonrevenue” sports.  
    
    2) I wonder what caused the added exposure to track and field athletes at the Olympics.  I also wonder why there are so many “nonrevenue” sports and so few major sports.     4) “Big leagues--big revenue, Little leagues--no revenue: The staggering wage differences among sports."

Although men's sports seem like they make more money than women's, there are also sports where women make more than men, like volleyball and soccer. 
    2) I wonder why some men make more in some sports when women make more in others. What causes that to happen? The graph says that it is because of the exposure from the Olympics, but wouldn't that mean that other sports get exposed too? Another thing I am wondering is why some sports don't have a gender specified, like wrestling, which doesn't specify.
    3) This impacts me and my community because it could impact which sports somebody may choose to play. For instance, maybe they see this graph, and then decide that they will pursue basketball, because it makes more money. It also impacts my community because this is what the people in my community are earning when they are "paid to play".
    4) Which sports do you get "paid to play" for? A look at the average earning for a college sports player and how your gender plays into that.

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
    (If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?)
    
    After analyzing the graph I noticed that there's a significant pay gap between men’s and women’s sports, especially in basketball and other major sports. Men's sports, particularly basketball, earn much more than women’s sports.
    
    2) What do you wonder?
    (Be Thoughtful! Can you relate your ideas to Statistics?)
    
    I wonder why certain sports like men's basketball earn so much more than others, and what factors determine a sport's ability to generate such high earnings. Could it be popularity, marketing, or something else? 
    
    3) How does this relate to you and your community?
    (This can be challenging - so think hard and make a good connection.) 
    
    This relates to my community because many of my peers aspire to play college sports, and they will be directly impacted by these earnings. It might influence their decisions about which sports to pursue seriously, knowing the potential earnings and opportunities available.
    
    4) What’s going on in this graph?
    (Create a short catchy INTERESTING headline that makes a reader want to read more)
    
    "Pay to Play: Unpacking the Gender Pay Gap in College Sports"

- The annotation text and arrow are explanatory callouts, not additional plotted data variables.
raw_comment:
The average earnings for college athletes is low for almost all sports besides Men's basketball and football, making substantial amounts. I wonder if this difference would be mitigated if college sports received more televised or online coverage. There is another blatant difference, that being the gender gap of pay throughout sports. The amount of sports making miniscule amounts is alarming, and I hope college athletes receive better/more sponsors to help them through their college journey. 
    I noticed the graph has no time scale which makes me wonder more. Presumably the scale is annually but still, low income college athletes playing ice hockey the whole year for 3 grand give or take is not a fair trade off.

1)The image presents two bar charts comparing the average earnings of college athletes in major and nonrevenue sports. In major sports, men's basketball players earn the most, averaging nearly $600,000, followed by football players with substantial but lower earnings. Women's basketball earnings are significantly lower than their male counterparts, and baseball players earn the least among major sports. In nonrevenue sports, men's golf leads in earnings, followed by women's gymnastics, while wrestling and both men's and women's track/cross country saw notable increases, attributed to Olympic exposure. However, earnings in nonrevenue sports remain significantly lower than in major sports, with the highest reaching around $20,000.

If you're a student-athlete or know one, understanding these earnings disparities could influence decisions about which sports to pursue, how to leverage NIL deals, or how to maximize financial opportunities.
    4)Show Me the Money! College Athletes Are Cashing In—But Who’s Winning?
